paragraphs: Seismologists once treated the faint, ceaseless vibration recorded even on quiet days as mere interference, a nuisance to be filtered out before the real signals of earthquakes could be read. That attitude has changed. The vibration, called microseismic noise, rises and falls with ocean storms, because colliding waves moving in opposite directions press on the sea floor and send energy into the crust. Because the noise is continuous and arrives from every direction, researchers can compare recordings at two stations and reconstruct how waves travel between them, in effect turning the ocean's restlessness into a free and tireless source for imaging the crust. The technique has real limits: it resolves shallow structure better than deep, and its results depend on noise sources being spread fairly evenly, which a single dominant storm can spoil. Still, a method that costs nothing to run deserves serious attention.
